extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of science fiction; prospective contributors and researchers interested in the magazine's editorial history
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes Asimov's Science Fiction magazine's editorial preferences, publication format choices, and historical selection practices relevant to writers aiming to publish short speculative fiction or researchers studying magazine markets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lean toward hard science fiction and straightforward style
rubrics_metrics.description: "we will lean toward hard science fiction, and toward the reasonably straightforward in the way of style..." (Asimov, editorial in the first issue)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asimov's stated early editorial goal favored 'hard' SF and clear, straightforward prose rather than highly experimental or New Wave material; the magazine planned to include humorous stories and occasional unclassifiable pieces but emphasized accessible, science-focused fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for traditional stories without sex or obscenity (Scithers era)
rubrics_metrics.description: George H. Scithers "favored traditional stories without sex or obscenity; along with frequent humorous stories, this gave Asimov's a reputation for printing juvenile fiction".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under Scithers the magazine prioritized conservative content (avoiding explicit sex/profanity), often publishing humor and material suitable to younger/new readers. This influenced submissions and perceptions of the magazine's target audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relaxation of prohibitions on sex and violence (McCarthy era)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shawna McCarthy "quickly relaxed the strictures on the kind of fiction Asimov's was willing to publish."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: McCarthy expanded the range of acceptable fiction to include stories involving sex and violence (e.g., Leigh Kennedy's "Her Furry Face", Octavia Butler's "Speech Sounds"). Her choices provoked reader complaints and cancellations but also produced award-winning work; editors should expect potential controversy when publishing boundary-pushing material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim to publish cutting-edge and wide-ranging speculative fiction (Dozois era)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gardner Dozois worked to solidify the impression that "Asimov's was where the 'cutting edge' work in the field was appearing" and printed a wide variety of speculative fiction, including cyberpunk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under Dozois the magazine favored innovative, high-quality contemporary SF across subgenres; editors programmed lead novellas and occasional serials and sought stories likely to be recognized in awards and 'Year's Best' anthologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a long novella as the lead story
rubrics_metrics.description: A regular feature of the magazine was a long novella as the lead story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Issues frequently opened with a substantial novella (lead slot) — writers targeting Asimov's should note that a prominent lead novella was a recurring editorial and design choice, and editors used it to anchor an issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective serialization policy (occasional, sometimes unpopular)
rubrics_metrics.description: Asimov's "had never run serials before Count Zero, and there was some resistance from the readers... Dozois persisted for a while... but those were the last to appear."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The magazine sometimes serialized novels (especially in the late 1980s), but serialization was infrequent and could meet reader resistance because serialized pieces often also appeared in book form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encouraging new writers and announcing first sales (early practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scithers "published many new writers" and his habit of announcing when a story was a first sale may have encouraged more submissions from new writers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically the magazine served as a market for debut authors and signaled first sales publicly, which attracted novice contributors; submission strategies that highlight first-time authorship can encourage new voices.

rubrics_metrics.name: High submission volume increases selectivity (Dozois era)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dozois received "hundreds of manuscripts a week, making it harder for new authors to break through."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As the magazine's reputation grew, submission volume increased significantly, raising editorial selectivity; new writers faced greater competition during high-reputation periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial mix includes non-fiction columns and puzzles (content-space tradeoffs)
rubrics_metrics.description: The magazine included features such as a Martin Gardner puzzle column, book reviews, opinion columns, and other non-fiction, which at times "took up space that could have been used for another story" (reader complaints).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors balance fiction with recurring non-fiction features; contributors should be aware that regular columns and puzzles may reduce fiction slots in an issue and influence editorial decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical payment and market positioning
rubrics_metrics.description: At one point Asimov's "was paying six cents per word, the same rate as its competitor, Analog Science Fiction/Science Fact."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The magazine historically offered competitive professional rates, a relevant factor for writers evaluating markets; pay rates and market positioning have changed over time and may affect submission decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format, frequency, and size as editorial constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Asimov's has been digest-sized throughout its history, with occasional size increases; publication frequency changed (quarterly, monthly, four-weekly, bimonthly double issues).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical format (digest size), page counts, and issue frequency (including double issues) shaped how many and what length of stories could be accepted; authors and editors must account for these production constraints when planning submissions and issue composition.
